claims.text: Adding 1–3 at.% Nb or Hf to a tungsten-rich refractory high-entropy alloy promotes dopant segregation to grain boundaries.
Nb or Hf grain-boundary segregation increases grain-boundary cohesion.
Nb or Hf segregation reduces excess free volume at grain boundaries.
The proposed dopant segregation retards high-temperature grain-boundary sliding.
The proposed dopant segregation retards grain-boundary decohesion at high temperature.
Improved grain-boundary cohesion delays crack initiation.
Improved grain-boundary cohesion delays crack propagation.
Delaying grain-boundary sliding, decohesion, and cracking permits greater high-temperature plastic deformation.
Delaying grain-boundary sliding, decohesion, and cracking increases high-temperature toughness.
Relative to an identically processed undoped alloy, the doped alloy will exhibit significantly greater ductility between 600 and 800 °C.
Relative to an identically processed undoped alloy, the doped alloy will exhibit significantly greater toughness between 600 and 800 °C.
The doped alloy will exhibit increased plastic-strain capacity and delayed failure during high-temperature mechanical testing.
A uniform dopant distribution without brittle intergranular phases is required for the predicted mechanical improvement.
The proposed mechanism applies to tungsten-based refractory high-entropy alloys fabricated by powder metallurgy and spark plasma sintering and tested at 600–800 °C.
The proposed mechanism may not apply to alloy systems with fundamentally different microstructures or processing histories.
